A study conducted in the Kathmandu Valley, Nepal, found that dietary consumption among children aged 12–23 months was associated with lower dietary adequacy and reduced length-for-age z-scores. This research was published in the Journal of Nutrition in October 2019 (PMID: 31309223; PMCID: PMC6768809). 2. The ENRICH Pakistan Project, led by Nutrition International in 2019, produced a formative research report detailing nutritional challenges and interventions in Pakistan. This report was complemented by associated publications, including work by Robert et al. 3. The Optifood study in Pakistan, conducted by UNICEF Pakistan and the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations, and Coordination in 2018, provided an analysis of dietary costs across 12 districts and 17 livelihood zones. This report highlighted the economic barriers to achieving optimal nutrition. 4. In Singapore, the GUSTO (Growing Up in Singapore Towards Healthy Outcomes) study examined food sources of energy and macronutrient intakes among infants aged 6–12 months. The findings, published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health in March 2018, emphasized the importance of early dietary patterns (PMID: 29534442; PMCID: PMC5877033). 5. The SMILING Project in Thailand, led by Chitchang et al., produced a country report in 2019 that explored dietary patterns and nutritional interventions. This report was informed by personal communications with Elaine Ferguson. 6. Similarly, the SMILING Project in Vietnam, led by Le Bach Mai et al., provided a country-specific report in 2019, detailing dietary practices and nutritional challenges. Elaine Ferguson also contributed to this report through direct communication. 7. The EU Childhood Obesity Project (CHOP) conducted a multi-country study across Belgium, Germany, Italy, Poland, and Spain. The research, published in the Journal of Nutrition in May 2018, demonstrated that unhealthy dietary patterns established during infancy often persist into mid-childhood, contributing to obesity risks (PMID: 29982656). 8. In Bulgaria, the National Center of Public Health and Analysis (NCPHA) provided a dataset on the nutritional status of children under five years of age. This dataset, harmonized by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), contributed to the Comprehensive European Food Consumption Database. 9. A study in the Czech Republic, published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition in February 2007, analyzed food consumption and feeding patterns among infants and toddlers in Prague. The findings highlighted regional dietary trends and their implications for child health (PMID: 16929247). 10. Research in France, published in the Journal of Nutrition in November 2016, revealed that infant exposure to sweetness and fattiness in diets increased during the first year of life. These dietary exposures were linked to specific feeding practices (PMID: 27733527). 11. The Dortmund Nutritional and Anthropometric Longitudinally Designed (DONALD) Study in Germany, conducted between 2006 and 2008, provided harmonized data for the European Food Safety Authority and the Global Dietary Database. 12. The Portuguese National Food, Nutrition, and Physical Activity Survey (IAN-AF) from 2015–2016, conducted by the University of Porto, contributed to the harmonization of dietary data for European and global databases. 13. In the United Kingdom, the Diet and Nutrition Survey of Infants and Young Children (DNSIYC) from 2011 provided critical insights into dietary patterns and nutritional status. This dataset, managed by the UK Data Service, was accessed for analysis in August 2021. 14. In Australia, research by Mauch et al., published in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Public Health in February 2017, examined portion sizes and food consumption frequency among children aged 14 and 24 months (PMID: 27960228). Another study by Byrne et al., published in Child Care Health and Development in May 2016, explored maternal perceptions of toddler weight status (PMID: 27001154). 15. In New Zealand, a study by Szymlek-Gay et al., published in Nutrition and Dietetics in 2010, quantified food consumption among children aged 12–24 months, providing valuable data on early childhood nutrition. 16. The development of food composition databases relied primarily on the USDA National Nutrient Database for Standard Reference (Release 28) and the USDA Food and Nutrient Database for Dietary Studies (2017–2018). When no suitable match was found, other national, regional, or project-specific databases were consulted, with a preference for data from the relevant country or region. 17. For fortified food items in the U.S. food supply, such as certain dairy and grain products, unfortified equivalents from the German national food composition database were used. This approach ensured consistency in nutrient data. 18. Food items were harmonized by selecting a single form (e.g., raw, cooked, or dry) to avoid discrepancies in water content and nutrient profiles. For example, legumes were standardized to their dry form, while vegetables were typically matched to their boiled and drained form. 19. Yield factors were applied to convert between raw and cooked forms of food, based on the ratio of dry matter content. These factors were computed using data from the USDA SR28 database. 20. Item clustering was employed to group similar food items, particularly when source datasets varied in specificity. This approach facilitated the matching of food items to nutrient composition data and ensured representation of foods consumed by at least 5% of children. 21. In cases where food items were poorly specified, representative items were selected or average items were created by averaging nutrient data across multiple sources. This method was used to address heterogeneity in food descriptions across datasets. 22. Special considerations were made for matching food items to nutrient composition data, particularly when items were consumed infrequently or lacked detailed descriptions. In such cases, clustering and representative item selection were used to ensure accurate modeling of dietary patterns.
